name: Top Bun Burger (comes on our best seven-grain bun)

recipe.history:
The story of multigrain and seven-grain breads stretches back thousands of years, winding through the ancient grain fields of the Fertile Crescent and the cereal-growing civilizations of the Near East. The earliest flatbreads baked by Neolithic peoples were already blended affairs — emmer wheat, einkorn, and barley ground together because the harvest made no distinction between varieties. It was the Egyptians who formalized leavened bread around 3000 BCE, and the Romans who spread the culture of varied-grain milling across Europe. In medieval Europe, peasant loaves were characteristically multigrain by necessity: rye, oat, millet, and spelt were milled together with whatever the season allowed, producing dense, hearty loaves that sustained laborers through long days of field work. The specific concept of a curated, intentional seven-grain blend — selecting complementary grains for flavor, texture, and nutrition — emerged more deliberately in Northern and Central Europe, particularly in Germany and Scandinavia, where dark, seeded, multi-grain breads like Vollkornbrot and Danish rugbrød became cultural cornerstones. These traditions valued the whole grain, the bran, and the germ as integral to both flavor and sustenance, a philosophy that would eventually travel west.

Multigrain breads arrived in American kitchens through waves of European immigration in the 19th and early 20th centuries, carried by German, Scandinavian, and Eastern European bakers who settled in the Midwest and opened neighborhood bakeries. For decades, however, the dominant American palate favored the soft, bleached white bread that industrialization made cheap and abundant — multigrain was the bread of immigrants and health reformers, not mainstream culture. That began to shift in the 1960s and 1970s, when the counterculture and back-to-the-land movements reclaimed whole and mixed grains as symbols of authenticity and wellness. By the 1980s and 1990s, artisan bakers and the burgeoning natural foods industry had elevated multigrain breads to grocery shelves nationwide. The burger world was slower to follow — for generations, the soft enriched white bun was the unquestioned vessel — but as burger culture grew more sophisticated through the 2000s and 2010s, chefs and home cooks alike began reaching for heartier, more flavorful buns. A seven-grain bun brought nuttiness, chew, and structural integrity that a standard white bun simply could not match, and suddenly the bun was no longer an afterthought but a statement.

I remember the first time a bun genuinely stopped me mid-bite. I was standing at a folding table at some weekend farmers market, holding a burger from a vendor I had only chosen because the line was short. The bun was seeded and dark at the crust, springy under my thumb in a way that felt alive, and when I bit through it the sweetness of toasted oat and the earthiness of whole wheat hit me before the beef did. It was autumn — I remember because there were gourds on the neighboring table and the air smelled like woodsmoke — and something about the nuttiness of that bread matched the season perfectly. I have been chasing that moment ever since. The Top Bun Burger is my attempt to honor it: to put the bun at the center of the equation, to insist that the foundation of a great burger is not an afterthought but an act of craft. Every time I mix the dough, I am back at that table, slightly surprised, completely won over.

A burger cooked to medium rare — an internal temperature of 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) — is not a preference; it is a conviction. At medium rare, the proteins in a beef patty have set just enough to hold the structure of the grind while leaving the interior yielding, juicy, and deeply beefy. The fat within the blend has begun to render but has not been driven out, which means every bite carries the full richness the butcher intended when that cut was selected. Above 140°F the muscle fibers tighten aggressively, moisture is expelled, and the patty becomes a compressed, drier version of itself — technically safe, culinarily diminished. The Maillard crust achieved on a screaming-hot cast iron or griddle surface provides all the caramelized, smoky depth a burger needs; the interior needs only warmth and surrender. To cook a burger past medium rare is to misunderstand what a burger is: not a well-done meatloaf slice, not a hockey puck of obligation, but a celebration of good beef treated with enough respect to be left mostly as nature arranged it. There is no correct way to serve a burger except pink in the middle, rested for two minutes, and eaten immediately.
ingredients: 120g bread flour, plus more for dusting
20g sunflower seeds, plus extra for topping
20g sesame seeds, plus extra for topping
1 tbsp neutral oil (such as sunflower or canola)
140g freshly ground beef blend: 60% chuck (80/20), 40% short rib
1/2 tsp neutral oil (for the griddle or cast iron)
2 leaves green leaf lettuce, washed and dried
3–4 thin slices white onion, separated into rings
2 small cucumbers, thinly sliced into rounds
instructions: 1. MAKE THE PICKLES (at least 2 hours ahead, ideally overnight): Toss the sliced cucumbers and onion with 1 tsp kosher salt in a colander set over a bowl. Let drain for 30 minutes, then rinse and pat dry. Combine the vinegar, water, sugar, mustard seeds, celery seeds, and turmeric in a small saucepan over medium heat, stirring until the sugar dissolves. Bring to a simmer, then remove from heat. Pack the cucumber and onion into a clean jar, pour the hot brine over them, let cool to room temperature, then refrigerate. Use after at least 2 hours; they keep for 2 weeks.

2. TOAST THE WHOLE GRAINS FOR THE BUN: In a dry skillet over medium heat, toast the rolled oats, millet, and amaranth together, stirring frequently, for 3–4 minutes until fragrant and lightly golden. Transfer to a bowl and let cool completely. Toast the flaxseeds and sunflower seeds in the same dry skillet for 2 minutes until just fragrant; add to the bowl with the oats. Reserve the sesame seeds separately for the topping.

3. BLOOM THE YEAST: Combine the warm water, honey, and active dry yeast in a large mixing bowl. Stir gently and let sit for 5–10 minutes until foamy. If the mixture does not foam, the yeast is inactive — discard and start again with fresh yeast.

4. MIX THE BUN DOUGH: Add the neutral oil to the bloomed yeast mixture. In a separate bowl, whisk together the bread flour, whole wheat flour, and rye flour with the fine sea salt. Add the flour mixture to the yeast mixture and stir with a wooden spoon until a shaggy dough forms. Add the toasted grain and seed mixture and stir to distribute evenly.

5. KNEAD THE DOUGH: Turn the dough out onto a lightly floured surface and knead vigorously for 8–10 minutes, until the dough is smooth, elastic, and only slightly tacky. The mixed grains will make it denser than an all-white dough — this is correct. Alternatively, use a stand mixer fitted with the dough hook on medium speed for 6 minutes.

6. FIRST RISE: Shape the kneaded dough into a ball, place it in a lightly oiled bowl, and cover tightly with plastic wrap or a damp towel. Let rise in a warm, draft-free spot (75–80°F / 24–27°C) for 1 to 1.5 hours, until roughly doubled in size.

7. SHAPE THE BUNS: Punch down the risen dough and turn it onto a lightly floured surface. Divide into 6 equal portions (approximately 90–95g each). Shape each portion into a tight round ball by pulling the dough taut over the top and pinching the seam firmly at the bottom. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, seam-side down, spacing them at least 2 inches apart.

8. SECOND RISE: Cover the shaped buns loosely with oiled plastic wrap and let proof at room temperature for 45–60 minutes, until noticeably puffed and the dough springs back slowly when poked with a fingertip.
9. PREHEAT THE OVEN: Preheat your oven to 375°F (190°C) with a rack in the center position.

10. EGG WASH AND TOP THE BUNS: Brush each bun generously with the beaten egg. Immediately sprinkle the tops with the reserved sesame seeds and a few additional sunflower seeds, pressing lightly so they adhere.

11. BAKE THE BUNS: Bake for 18–22 minutes, rotating the pan once halfway through, until the buns are deep golden brown and sound hollow when tapped on the bottom. Transfer to a wire rack and cool for at least 20 minutes before slicing. Do not rush this step — steam inside the bun needs to redistribute.

12. MAKE THE HOMEMADE MAYONNAISE: In a medium bowl, whisk together the egg yolk, Dijon mustard, white wine vinegar, and salt until smooth and slightly thickened. Begin adding the neutral oil drop by drop while whisking constantly. Once the emulsion has formed and the mixture is visibly thick (after about 3 tablespoons of oil), add the remaining oil in a slow, thin, steady stream, whisking continuously. The finished mayonnaise should be thick, pale, and glossy. Taste and adjust salt. Refrigerate until needed.

13. MAKE THE SPECIAL SAUCE: Combine 60ml of the homemade mayonnaise with the yellow mustard, ketchup, finely minced dill pickle, apple cider vinegar, smoked paprika, garlic powder, onion powder, and cayenne. Stir until fully combined and smooth. Taste and adjust seasoning. Cover and refrigerate until ready to assemble.

14. PREPARE THE PATTY: Remove the ground beef blend from the refrigerator 20 minutes before cooking to take the chill off. Divide into 140g portions. Handle the meat as little as possible — overworking compresses the grind and produces a dense, rubbery patty. Form each portion into a round patty approximately 4 inches (10cm) in diameter and 3/4 inch (2cm) thick. Use your thumb to press a shallow dimple into the center of each patty to prevent it from doming as it cooks. Season both sides generously with kosher salt and black pepper immediately before cooking.

15. COOK THE PATTY TO MEDIUM RARE: Heat a cast iron skillet or heavy griddle over high heat until it begins to smoke lightly. Add the neutral oil and swirl to coat. Lay the patty down gently and do not move it for 2.5–3 minutes, until a deep mahogany crust has formed on the bottom. Flip once. Cook the second side for 2–2.5 minutes. In the final 60 seconds of cooking, lay the slice of sharp cheddar on top of the patty and tent loosely with a metal bowl or pan lid to trap heat and melt the cheese. Pull the patty off the heat when an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part reads 130–135°F (54–57°C). This is medium rare. It is the only correct target temperature for a burger patty. Transfer to a wire rack or plate and rest for 2 full minutes before assembling.

16. TOAST THE BUN: While the patty rests, split the baked seven-grain bun in half. Place both cut sides down in the same hot skillet used for the patty — do not wipe it out, the rendered beef fat will add flavor. Toast for 60–90 seconds until golden and lightly crisped.

17. ASSEMBLE THE BURGER: Spread a generous tablespoon of special sauce on the cut face of the bottom bun. Layer the green leaf lettuce on the sauce — it acts as a moisture barrier and keeps the bun from going soggy. Place the tomato slices on the lettuce, followed by the white onion rings. Set the rested, cheese-topped patty directly on the onion. Arrange 4–5 bread-and-butter pickle chips on top of the patty. Spread a thin layer of special sauce on the cut face of the top bun and place it sauce-side down to close the burger.

18. SERVE IMMEDIATELY: The burger must be eaten within 3–4 minutes of assembly while the patty is still warm and the bun still has its crust. Serve with additional pickles and extra special sauce on the side.
